(2024) Yes No No No Wu et al. (2024) Yes No No No Ours Yes Yes Yes Yes Table 1: Comparison with prior work on LLM reasoning robustness. Prior studies mainly evaluate behavioral sensitivity under perturbations, whereas our work adds mechanistic diagnosis, failure taxonomy, and repair validation. 3 Methodology Our methodology consists of three stages: (1) constructing a controlled perturbation dataset from GSM8K, (2) evaluating model robustness via paired inference, and (3) applying mechanistic interpretability techniques to diagnose the internal causes of failure. Figure 1: Overview of MPD. We construct meaning-preserving perturbation pairs from GSM8K, evaluate paired robustness across models, and diagnose failures with logit lens, activation patching, component ablation, and the Cascading Amplification Index (CAI). 3.1 Perturbation Dataset Construction We construct a dataset of 677 valid problem pairs from the GSM8K test set ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) , each consisting of an original problem and a meaning-preserving variant. We apply two perturbation types: name substitution (341 pairs), where all character names are replaced with randomly sampled alternatives, and number format paraphrasing (336 pairs), where numerical expressions are rephrased into equivalent formats (e.g., “ $5 ” → \rightarrow “ 5 dollars ”, “ 60% ” → \rightarrow “ 60 percent ”). Both types preserve the mathematical structure and correct answer. We discard any pair where the perturbation introduces ambiguity. 3.2 Paired Robustness Evaluation For each model, we perform greedy decoding (temperature = 0) on both the original and perturbed problem using a fixed prompt instructing the model to solve the problem and output the answer after a #### delimiter. A sample ( q , q ′ ) (q,q^{\prime}) is a flip if the model answers the original correctly but the perturbed variant incorrectly: flip ( q , q ′ ) = 𝟙 [ f ( q ) = a ∗ ] ⋅ 𝟙 [ f ( q ′ ) ≠ a ∗ ] \text{flip}(q,q^{\prime})=\mathbb{1}[f(q)=a^{*}]\cdot\mathbb{1}[f(q^{\prime})\neq a^{*}] (1) 3.3 Mechanistic Analysis We apply three complementary interpretability techniques to the subset of flipped samples. 3.3.1 Logit Lens Analysis The logit lens ( nostalgebraist, 2020 ) projects the hidden state at each layer l l through the unembedding matrix W U W_{U} : p ( l ) = softmax ​ ( W U ⋅ h ( l ) ) p^{(l)}=\text{softmax}(W_{U}\cdot h^{(l)}) (2) We identify the first divergence layer : the earliest layer at which the top-1 predicted token differs between the original and perturbed inputs, and compare distributions using a Mann-Whitney U U test. Figure 2: Logit lens applied to a flipped sample and a stable sample from Mistral-7B ( Jiang et al., 2023 ) . JSD rises sharply for the flip case but remains near zero for the stable case. 3.3.2 Activation Patching For each flipped sample and each layer l l , we replace the hidden states at diverging token positions with those from the original (correct) forward pass: h ~ t ( l ) = { h orig , t ( l ) if ​ t ∈ 𝒯 div h pert , t ( l ) otherwise \tilde{h}^{(l)}_{t}=\begin{cases}h^{(l)}_{\text{orig},t}&\text{if }t\in\mathcal{T}_{\text{div}}\\ h^{(l)}_{\text{pert},t}&\text{otherwise}\end{cases} (3) A high recovery rate indicates localized failures; a low rate indicates distributed sensitivity. 3.3.3 Component Ablation For each layer l l , we zero out the output of either the attention sublayer or MLP sublayer: h ( l ) = h ( l − 1 ) + Attn ( l ) ​ ( h ( l − 1 ) ) + MLP ( l ) ​ ( h ( l − 1 ) ) h^{(l)}=h^{(l-1)}+\text{Attn}^{(l)}(h^{(l-1)})+\text{MLP}^{(l)}(h^{(l-1)}) (4) If ablating component c c at layer l l yields the correct answer, then c ( l ) c^{(l)} was causally contributing to the failure. 3.3.4 Cascading Amplification Index To quantify whether layer-wise divergence amplifies or attenuates across the network, we introduce the Cascading Amplification Index (CAI): CAI = 1 L − l 0 ∑ l = l 0 L − 1 𝟙 [ Δ l + 1 > Δ l ] \text{CAI}=\frac{1}{L-l_{0}}\sum_{l=l_{0}}^{L-1}\mathbb{1}[\Delta_{l+1}>\Delta_{l}] (5) where Δ l = JSD ( p orig ( l ) ∥ p pert ( l ) ) \Delta_{l}=\text{JSD}(p^{(l)}_{\text{orig}}\|p^{(l)}_{\text{pert}}) is the divergence between logit lens projections at layer l l , and l 0 l_{0} is the first divergence layer. CAI ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \in[0,1] : values near 1 indicate persistent amplification, values near 0 indicate self-correction. 4 Experimental Setup We evaluate three open-weight instruction-tuned LLMs: Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 ( Jiang et al., 2023 ) (7B parameters, 32 layers), Llama-3-8B-Instruct ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) (8B parameters, 32 layers), and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct ( Qwen et al., 2025 ) (7B parameters, 28 layers). All models are loaded in float16 precision with greedy decoding. For each model, we select the first 60 flipped samples as the mechanistic analysis subset. Logit lens is applied to all 677 pairs; activation patching and component ablation are applied to the 60-sample subset. All experiments are conducted on a university HPC cluster with NVIDIA GPUs. 5 Results 5.1 Perturbation Robustness Model Overall Name Number Mistral-7B 45.1% 27.3% 63.1% Llama-3-8B 33.5% 23.5% 43.8% Qwen2.5-7B 28.8% 18.2% 39.6% Table 2: Flip rates by model and perturbation type. All three models exhibit substantial sensitivity to meaning-preserving perturbations (Table 2 ). Number format paraphrasing is consistently more disruptive, with the disparity particularly pronounced for Mistral-7B ( Jiang et al., 2023 ) (63.1% vs. 27.3%). 5.2 Logit Lens Analysis Model Flip No-Flip p p r r Mistral-7B 9.1 11.6 2.07e-04 0.157 Llama-3-8B 13.0 14.7 2.14e-02 0.451 Qwen2.5-7B 17.2 19.5 9.23e-06 0.395 Table 3: Mean first divergence layer for flipped vs. non-flipped samples. All comparisons significant at p < 0.05 p<0.05 . Flipped samples diverge at significantly earlier layers across all three models (Table 3 ). Mistral-7B shows the earliest divergence (layer 9.1), consistent with its highest flip rate. Figure 3: Distribution of first divergence layers for flipped vs. non-flipped samples. 5.3 Activation Patching Model Recovery Rate Mistral-7B 3/60 5.0% Llama-3-8B 43/60 71.7% Qwen2.5-7B 0/60 0.0% Table 4: Activation patching recovery rates. Activation patching reveals a stark architectural divide (Table 4 ): Llama-3 is highly recoverable (71.7%), whereas Mistral (5.0%) and Qwen (0.0%) are not. Figure 4: Activation patching recovery rate by layer. 5.4 Component Ablation Model Attn Recov. MLP Recov. Attn Mean MLP Mean Attn First MLP First Mistral-7B 27/60 (45%) 21/60 (35%) 1.13 0.78 11.8 14.9 Llama-3-8B 45/60 (75%) 46/60 (77%) 5.78 4.95 6.4 8.0 Qwen2.5-7B 24/60 (40%) 29/60 (48%) 1.75 2.15 5.2 3.9 Table 5: Component ablation results. Recov. = samples with at least one recovering layer. Mean = mean recovering layers per sample. First = mean first recovery layer. Component ablation reveals architecture-specific patterns (Table 5 ). In Mistral, attention is the dominant causal component (27/60 vs. 21/60, earlier recovery at layer 11.8 vs. 14.9). Llama-3 shows high recovery from both components, consistent with localized failures. Qwen reverses the pattern: MLP sublayers recover more samples (29/60 vs. 24/60) at earlier layers (3.9 vs. 5.2). Figure 5: Per-layer recovery under component ablation. Mistral and Llama-3 show attention dominance, while Qwen shows MLP dominance. 6 Discussion 6.1 Cascading Amplification Figure 6: Mean layer-wise JSD trajectory for flipped vs. stable samples. Flipped samples exhibit cascading amplification; stable samples show attenuation. Figure 6 shows the layer-wise JSD trajectory for flipped vs. stable samples. For stable samples, JSD remains low as the model attenuates the perturbation. For flipped samples, JSD amplifies through later layers, with the flip-to-stable ratio growing from ∼ 1.7 × {\sim}1.7\times at layer 4 to 9.9 × 9.9\times at the final layer for Mistral ( Jiang et al., 2023 ) . Flipped samples exhibit significantly higher CAI across all three models (Table 6 ). CAI outperforms first divergence layer as a failure predictor for Mistral (AUC 0.679 vs. 0.579) and Llama-3 ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) (0.593 vs. 0.540), while first divergence layer is slightly more predictive for Qwen ( Qwen et al., 2025 ) (0.605 vs. 0.560). Model Flip Stable p p r r Mistral-7B 0.616 0.545 2.86e-15 0.357 Llama-3-8B 0.548 0.511 7.39e-05 0.186 Qwen2.5-7B 0.500 0.472 1.06e-02 0.121 Table 6: CAI for flipped vs. stable samples. This cascading dynamic explains the patching results: in Llama-3, the cascade passes through a narrow bottleneck that patching can interrupt; in Mistral and Qwen, it spreads through redundant pathways. 6.2 Mechanistic Failure Taxonomy Our analysis reveals three qualitatively distinct failure profiles (Table 7 ). Property Mistral Llama-3 Qwen Flip rate 45.1% 33.5% 28.8% Patch recovery 5.0% 71.7% 0.0% Dominant comp. Attn Attn MLP First diverge 9.1 13.0 17.2 Failure type Distributed Localized Entangled Table 7: Architecture-specific failure profiles. Localized (Llama-3). Moderate flip rate (33.5%) but highly recoverable failures (71.7% patching recovery). Perturbation-sensitive information flows through a narrow computational pathway. Distributed (Mistral). Highest flip rate (45.1%) with near-zero patching recovery (5.0%). Attention heads at middle-to-late layers are disproportionately causal, but the effect is redundantly encoded across layers. Entangled (Qwen). Zero patching recovery with reversed component dominance: MLP sublayers, not attention, are the primary causal components. Perturbation sensitivity is distributed across both layers and components. We formalize these as: Localized ( R patch > 0.5 R_{\text{patch}}>0.5 ), Distributed ( R patch < 0.1 R_{\text{patch}}<0.1 , R attn > R mlp R_{\text{attn}}>R_{\text{mlp}} ), and Entangled ( R patch < 0.1 R_{\text{patch}}<0.1 , R mlp > R attn R_{\text{mlp}}>R_{\text{attn}} ). 6.3 Taxonomy Validation via Targeted Repair To validate that the taxonomy is actionable, we implement targeted repair strategies guided by each model’s failure profile and evaluate whether repair difficulty follows the predicted ordering: localized > > distributed ≈ \approx entangled. Model Strategy Recovery Rate Llama-3 Layer FT (L3–5) 25/222 11.3% Steering ( α \alpha =0.5) 27/222 12.2% Qwen Layer FT (L0,2,5) 14/195 7.2% Steering ( α \alpha =1.0) 14/195 7.2% ROME MLP edit − - 2/180 − - 1.1% Mistral Layer FT (L12,14,27) 15/305 4.9% Steering ( α \alpha =0.5) 16/305 5.2% Table 8: Repair results. Recovery = previously-flipped samples now correct. Negative recovery indicates regression. Layer Fine-Tuning. We freeze all parameters except mechanistically-identified target layers and fine-tune with a combined cross-entropy and representational alignment loss. For Llama-3, fine-tuning layers 3–5 (8.2% of parameters) recovers 11.3% of failures. Steering Vectors. We compute per-layer correction vectors as the mean hidden-state difference between original and perturbed inputs ( Turner et al., 2024 ) , requiring no training. Steering recovers 12.2% for Llama-3, 7.2% for Qwen, and 5.2% for Mistral. ROME Editing. Rank-one MLP weight updates ( Meng et al., 2023 ) applied to Qwen produce negative recovery ( − - 1.1%), with most edited samples generating malformed outputs, demonstrating that entangled failures resist localized weight surgery. Results. The repair results (Table 8 ) confirm the taxonomy’s predictive validity. Localized failures (Llama-3) are the most repairable: two independent methods each recover > > 11%. Entangled failures (Qwen) plateau at ∼ \sim 7% regardless of method. Distributed failures (Mistral) yield the lowest recovery (5.2%), consistent with the absence of any single correctable bottleneck. 7 Conclusion We presented a mechanistic analysis of LLM sensitivity to meaning-preserving perturbations. By combining logit lens, activation patching, component ablation, and CAI into the MPD framework, we diagnosed where and how failures arise within model internals. Our central finding is that reasoning fragility manifests through architecture-specific failure modes, namely localized (Llama-3 ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) , 71.7% patching recovery), distributed (Mistral ( Jiang et al., 2023 ) , 5.0%), and entangled (Qwen ( Qwen et al., 2025 ) , 0.0%), which we formalize as a mechanistic taxonomy. The Cascading Amplification Index significantly predicts failure across all three architectures (AUC up to 0.679). Critically, the taxonomy predicts repair difficulty: targeted interventions recover 12.2% of localized failures but only 5–7% of distributed and entangled failures, validating the taxonomy as actionable. Future work should explore whether these failure modes persist at larger scales, generalize to other reasoning domains, and whether combining multiple taxonomy-guided interventions can improve recovery rates. Limitations Our mechanistic analysis is restricted to 60 flipped samples per model due to computational constraints. We evaluate only 7–8B parameter models; scaling behavior is unknown. Our perturbation types are limited to name substitution and number paraphrasing. Component ablation uses zero-ablation, which may not reflect natural causal structure. Finally, our analysis focuses on the answer token position; perturbation effects may also manifest at earlier reasoning steps. LLM Usage Disclosure We used an LLM assistant to help with experiment implementation and paper drafting. All experimental results were independently verified by the authors, and all scientific claims and interpretations are the authors’ own. Ethics Statement Our work studies existing open-weight models on a public benchmark (GSM8K) and does not involve human subjects. Name substitution pools are designed to avoid demographic bias. All perturbations are meaning-preserving and do not introduce harmful content. We will release our perturbation dataset and analysis code upon acceptance to support reproducibility. assessment.writer_rationale:
**+1 Likely feasible, confidence 0.82:** for the approximately three-month feasibility assessment, a relevant interpretability lab is likely to achieve all six criteria with one frozen configuration. Confidence is limited because each experiment used one fixed set of random seeds; the reported intervals do not estimate variability across new development-data partitions.

**A development-frozen six-criterion pass would move the score to +2 Feasible.** Conversely, replicated matched results in which adequate recipient decoding consistently accompanies inadequate repair or excessive disruption—or successful repair consistently leaves decoding below its threshold—would move the assessment toward balance or likely infeasibility.

### Why not the neighbouring scores

**+2 Feasible would treat a demonstrated readout obstacle as routine:** the converged recipient decoder's substantial shortfall shows that this step is sensitive to implementation. **0 Evenly balanced would discount the diversity of successful repair:** two donor-selection rules and token scopes worked, so the positive case does not depend on one head-selection recipe.

payload.claim_text: On 1,200 held-out file-transfer problems balanced between permitted and forbidden requests, with four files and four recipients, linear decoders of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct's final prompt-token residual state identify the requested file and its permitted recipient with at least 90% accuracy each, even among incorrect authorization decisions. Patching a fixed set of at most 12 attention heads from correct runs containing the same permission facts in reordered table rows corrects at least 30% of all initial errors while changing no more than 3% of correct decisions. Decoders, heads, and donor-selection rules are fixed on separate development data, with decoders trained on both correct and incorrect development runs; test names and permission assignments are unseen.

subclaims.text: Linear decoding of the final prompt-token residual state identifies the requested file with at least 90% accuracy across the full held-out test set.
subclaims.experiment_hint: Extract final prompt-token residual states from development runs, train a linear requested-file decoder using ground-truth labels, freeze it, and evaluate its predictions on all 1,200 held-out states.

subclaims.text: Linear decoding of the final prompt-token residual state identifies the requested file's permitted recipient with at least 90% accuracy across the full held-out test set.
subclaims.experiment_hint: Train a linear permitted-recipient decoder on development final prompt-token residual states and task ground-truth labels. Freeze the decoder and evaluate recipient-label accuracy over all 1,200 test problems.

subclaims.text: The frozen requested-file decoder achieves at least 90% accuracy among held-out problems on which the model initially makes an incorrect authorization decision.
subclaims.experiment_hint: Compare unpatched authorization decisions with task ground truth to identify the error subset. Without retraining or selecting another decoder, calculate requested-file accuracy on that subset using the original final prompt-token residual states.

subclaims.text: The frozen permitted-recipient decoder achieves at least 90% accuracy among held-out problems on which the model initially makes an incorrect authorization decision.
subclaims.experiment_hint: Use the initial-error subset determined from unpatched authorization decisions. Apply the already-frozen permitted-recipient decoder to its original final prompt-token residual states and score against task ground truth.

subclaims.text: Patching the fixed attention-head set from qualifying correct donor runs corrects at least 30% of all initial authorization errors.
subclaims.experiment_hint: Record initial decisions, obtain donor activations using the frozen donor-selection rules, and patch the fixed head set. Compare patched decisions with ground truth, using every initial error—not merely errors with successful patches—as the correction-rate denominator.

subclaims.text: The same fixed attention-head patching intervention changes no more than 3% of initially correct authorization decisions.
subclaims.experiment_hint: Evaluate the same frozen intervention on the initially correct cases. Compare each patched authorization decision with its original decision and divide the number changed by the total number of initially correct cases; do not count mere wording changes as authorization-decision changes.

Donor-generation and fixed donor-selection algorithm, candidate row permutations, search budget, and handling of unavailable qualifying donors.

payload.thought:
**Claim Card — locked before search**

- **System/model:** Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with frozen pretrained weights; development-trained linear decoders and development-selected attention-head interventions.
- **Property:** Accurate decoding of task-relevant entities, including on authorization errors, plus selective causal correction through donor activation patching.
- **Conditions:** 1,200 held-out problems; four files and four recipients; 600 permitted and 600 forbidden requests; unseen test names and permission assignments. Decoders are trained on both correct and incorrect development runs. Decoder parameters, at most 12 patched heads, and donor-selection rules are frozen before testing. Donors preserve the permission facts but reorder table rows and must produce correct decisions.
- **Quantifier:** Existential feasibility for this model and task, not a guarantee across arbitrary prompts or datasets.
- **Thresholds:** SC1–SC2 require at least 1,080 correct predictions each. For E initial authorization errors, SC3–SC4 require at least ceil(0.90E) correct predictions each, and SC5 requires at least ceil(0.30E) corrections. For C initially correct decisions, SC6 permits at most floor(0.03C) changed decisions.
- **Comparator:** The same model’s unpatched authorization decisions and original final prompt-token activations.
- **Operational assumptions:** Authorization is scored as a binary decision under a fixed evaluation protocol. Each requested file has a well-defined permitted recipient. Decoder outputs identify candidates within each problem, rather than requiring a fixed classifier to output previously unseen literal names; the candidate-indexing convention must be specified and fixed without leaking the answer. The residual extraction location and patch-position/alignment rules must also be fixed on development data. Missing qualifying donors count as unsuccessful corrections, not excluded errors. Error-subset metrics require a nonempty initial-error subset.
- **Decisive evidence:** A matched, leakage-controlled evaluation meeting all six thresholds would establish feasibility. Evidence against the two error-subset decoding thresholds or the selective patching thresholds would weigh strongly against it. Failure of one selected implementation alone would not prove that every permitted implementation is infeasible.

**Decomposition and pre-check**

All six supplied subclaims are experimental and conjunctive: SC1 AND SC2 AND SC3 AND SC4 AND SC5 AND SC6. SC3 and SC5 are designated bottlenecks; every stated threshold remains necessary.

SC1–SC4 share one activation-extraction and frozen-probe evaluation pipeline. SC5–SC6 share one development-selected intervention evaluated on both initially wrong and initially correct cases. A faithful experiment would likely require hours to days, depending on development-set size, donor search, hardware, and patch-position choices.

The claim is internally possible: changing table order preserves semantic facts while potentially changing attention computations. No obvious impossibility theorem rules out these finite-task thresholds. However, successful linear decoding does not establish that the model causally uses the decoded information, and correcting errors does not establish low collateral damage. These require separate evidence. Candidate indexing is a material ambiguity because literal-name classification with unseen output classes would be a different task.

Only search and finish are available in this interface; no computation or cluster tool is exposed. I will therefore look for matched published experiments and closely related evidence, explicitly distinguishing them from experiments actually run. The first search serves all six subclaims and prioritizes the exact model, authorization task, probing, and patching mechanism.

observation.why: Closest primary study of error-conditioned binding decoding and causal repair, but important mismatches remain: its task is entity–obligation retrieval, not file-transfer permission, and its 7B checkpoint is Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B, not Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Multinomial linear probes read the final query-position residual stream. For Qwen2.5-7B, failure-conditioned probe accuracy is 27.6% (seed range 23.6–34.5%), against a 12.5% present-obligation baseline. The decoding experiment uses 200 training, 200 validation, and 200 untouched test trials per seed, with refitting on training plus validation. Repair instead adds a class-mean residual direction toward the probe-decoded obligation; it does not patch a fixed attention-head set from reordered-context donors. In the separate repair configuration, Table 5 reports 29% error correction and 79% correct-trial preservation, implying 21% correct-to-incorrect collateral change; accuracy rises from 36.0% to 47.2%. Repair-layer selection uses validation failures, not test outcomes. Probe accuracy establishes decodability, while the intervention supplies separate causal evidence. These findings do not verify the requested recipient-decoding or selective head-repair claim.

observation.citation: “Through extensive experiments on nine models and ten binding tasks, we uncover a consistent pattern in how LMs mix these mechanisms to drive model behavior.”

It distinguishes positional, lexical, and reflexive retrieval routes using counterfactual activation interchange, rather than relying only on attention visualization. Binding information is studied through interventions on the last-token residual stream before retrieval. However, these are templated entity-retrieval tasks, including boxes and music, not file-transfer permission decisions. Counterfactual donors deliberately make retrieval mechanisms predict different entities; this is not evidence that semantically equivalent reordered-context donors selectively repair naturally incorrect decisions. The reported approximately 95% agreement concerns a causal model's prediction of next-token distributions, not an error-correction rate. The source does not establish the requested error-subset entity-and-recipient linear-probe results, a fixed small repair-head set, corresponding correction/collateral-change rates, or development/test separation for that repair protocol. Prioritize Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct where available. Distinguish decoding at entity tokens from decoding at the final prompt token, and overall accuracy from accuracy conditioned on incorrect model answers. For interventions, extract head counts, whether the same heads are used across held-out examples, donor semantics, natural-error correction rates, and changes to initially correct answers. observation.citation: we collected hidden state activations at entity token positions as well as at final token positions at every layer
observation.why: Gur-Arieh, Geva and Geiger, Mixing Mechanisms, provides experiments including Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Appendix B.2 uses multinomial logistic regression at entity tokens and final tokens separately. Crucially, the decoded variable is entity-group position—not the complete entity–attribute binding. Middle positions become less separable as context grows. Counterfactual residual-stream interchange experiments distinguish positional, lexical and reflexive retrieval mechanisms; they are not small-head selective repair experiments. The paper does not report natural-error correction or initially-correct-answer damage for a fixed head set patched from semantically identical reordered-table donors. Its approximately 95% distributional agreement concerns a causal model of retrieval, not failure-conditioned decoding accuracy. Thus it supports accessible positional information and causal retrieval mechanisms, but not the stronger repair claim. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.06182v1))

observation.citation: On the trials each model gets wrong, probe accuracy exceeds the strict present-obligation baseline, 1/K = 0.125
observation.why: Ravulapalli, Chadha and Hari, Legible Failures, directly tests binding decoding conditioned on incorrect answers, using final-query-position residual states and disjoint training, validation and test folds. The relevant checkpoint is Qwen2.5-7B BASE, not Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. For K=8, D=64, model accuracy is 57.1%; probe accuracy conditioned on model errors is 27.6% (seed range 23.6–34.5%), versus 12.5% chance. These are different quantities. In a separate K=6, D=256 steering experiment, Qwen2.5-7B accuracy rises from 36.0% to 47.2%; the decoded arm repairs 29% of wrong trials and preserves 79% of initially correct trials. The intervention changes residual vectors toward a probe-decoded binding; there is no attention-head set or reordered-table donor. Consequently, this is evidence for failure-conditioned accessibility and residual-steering repair, not selective repair through fixed heads. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.11216v1))

observation.citation: We further show that binding ID vectors form a continuous subspace
observation.why: Feng and Steinhardt, How do Language Models Bind Entities in Context?, is the foundational primary experimental source. It studies Pythia and LLaMA, not Qwen2.5. Entity- and attribute-position activation substitutions and additive mean interventions establish causally effective binding-ID directions; this is not a supervised final-prompt-token binding-decoding result. Interventions intentionally switch associations, erase binding information or restore artificially erased information. The reported above-97% accuracy when simultaneous entity and attribute interventions cancel is not a natural-error correction rate. The work neither identifies a small fixed attention-head set nor measures preservation of initially correct answers under reordered-table donor patching. Attention heads comparing binding IDs are explicitly proposed as a possible mechanism rather than experimentally isolated here. It supports linear/additive binding representations, not the complete selective-repair claim. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/html/2310.17191v2))

Circuit components are head–token-position pairs: groups operate at final, query-label and previous-query-label positions. The discovered 72-head circuit is evaluated without per-example reselection and transferred unchanged across models; separately discovered Goat/FLoat circuits contain 175 heads. The unchanged circuit retains 97%, 89% and 88% of full-model performance in Vicuna, Goat and FLoat respectively—faithfulness ratios, not percentages of natural errors repaired. Discovery uses original/noise pairs, semantic tests use counterfactual donors, and cross-model patching uses another model's activations on the same input. None is semantically identical reordered-table donor repair. The paper does not provide the requested wrong-to-correct and correct-to-wrong rates, nor establish them through entity-token versus final-token linear decoding. payload.thought:
## Feasibility judgment

**Likely infeasible as the complete joint numerical claim (−1), with low-to-moderate confidence, approximately 60%.** This is a feasibility projection, **not a demonstrated failure**: no matched experiment establishes or contradicts all six thresholds.

The strongest concerns are accurate permitted-recipient decoding **conditioned on authorization errors**, and achieving substantial error correction with **≤3% disturbance of correct decisions**. Related experiments demonstrate accessible binding information and causal interventions, but their failure-conditioned decoding and intervention selectivity fall substantially short. However, their tasks and interventions differ materially, and the claimed four-candidate instruction-tuned setting could be considerably easier.

**No computational experiment was executed.** The available interface provided search but no execution tool. All numerical evidence below comes from retrieved research reports.

## Claim Card

- **System:** Frozen Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct; development-trained linear decoders; a development-selected set of at most 12 attention heads.
- **Capability:** Decode the requested file and its permitted recipient from the final prompt-token residual state, including on incorrect authorization decisions; selectively repair decisions using correct, semantically equivalent row-reordered donors.
- **Conditions:** 1,200 held-out problems, 600 permitted and 600 forbidden, four files and four recipients. Test names and permission assignments are unseen in development. Decoders include correct and incorrect development runs in training. Decoders, heads, and donor-selection rules are frozen before evaluation.
- **Quantifier:** Existential feasibility for this model and task—not robustness across arbitrary prompt formats.
- **Thresholds:** SC1–SC2 each require at least 1,080/1,200 correct predictions. With E initial errors and C initially correct decisions, SC3–SC4 each require at least ceil(0.90E) correct predictions; SC5 requires at least ceil(0.30E) repairs; SC6 permits at most floor(0.03C) changed authorization decisions.
- **Comparator:** The same model’s original, unpatched activations and decisions.
- **Decisive evidence:** A leakage-controlled, frozen evaluation meeting every threshold would establish feasibility. A matched failure would contradict that implementation; rejecting the broader existential claim would require evidence that the failure is not merely implementation-specific.

**Pre-check:** No logical inconsistency or applicable impossibility theorem was identified. Linear accessibility, causal use, and selective repair are distinct properties and must not be conflated.

## Subclaims and evidence

All six subclaims are **experimental** and connected by **AND**. SC3 and SC5 are designated bottlenecks; every other threshold also remains necessary.

| Subclaim | Evidence and assessment |
|---|---|
| **SC1: Requested-file decoding ≥90% overall** | No matched measurement. Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct retrieval research reports linear accessibility of entity-position information, including at final-token positions, but not this requested-file metric. This is the most plausible component, but remains unverified. |
| **SC2: Permitted-recipient decoding ≥90% overall** | Binding representations and causal retrieval mechanisms have experimental support. Nevertheless, decoding position or applicability is not equivalent to identifying the requested file’s associated recipient. No matched measurement establishes 90%. |
| **SC3: Requested-file decoding ≥90% on initial errors — bottleneck** | No matched error-subset measurement. Correctly representing the explicitly requested file could coexist with an incorrect authorization judgment, but the necessary frequency has not been measured. **Not demonstrated to pass or fail.** |
| **SC4: Permitted-recipient decoding ≥90% on initial errors** | The closest failure-conditioned binding study reports only **27.6%** decoding accuracy for Qwen2.5-7B base, versus 12.5% chance. This is a quantitative warning, but its eight-candidate, distractor-containing task and base checkpoint differ substantially from the claim. **Concerning, not a matched contradiction.** |
| **SC5: Fixed ≤12-head intervention repairs ≥30% of all errors — bottleneck** | Related studies establish causal manipulation of bindings, but none retrieved evaluates the specified fixed-head, reordered-table donor protocol. A separate residual-steering experiment repairs **29%** of errors, showing that meaningful repair is possible, not that this head-patching threshold is met. **Unverified.** |
| **SC6: Intervention changes ≤3% of initially correct decisions** | No matched measurement. The same residual-steering experiment preserves **79%** of correct trials, implying 21% damage—far above 3%, but under a different intervention and task. This is the strongest quantitative warning about selectivity. **Unverified, with adverse analogous evidence.** |

### Relevant primary sources

1. **[Legible Failures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11216)**  
   Uses disjoint training, validation, and test folds and final-query residual probes. For **Qwen2.5-7B base**, failure-conditioned binding accuracy is **27.6%**, with a reported seed range of **23.6–34.5%**, in an eight-candidate setting. A separate six-candidate residual-steering configuration reports **29% error repair** and **79% correct-trial preservation**. These are not measurements of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct file-transfer authorization or attention-head donor patching.

2. **[Mixing Mechanisms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.06182)**  
   Includes Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and demonstrates positional, lexical, and reflexive retrieval mechanisms through causal interventions. Its linear probes decode entity-group position, not complete file–recipient bindings. Its reported approximately 95% causal-model agreement is **not** a decoding or natural-error-repair rate.

3. **[How do Language Models Bind Entities in Context?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.17191)**  
   Establishes linearly structured, causally effective binding representations in other model families. Association switching and restoration after artificial erasure support the mechanism, but do not establish high decoding accuracy on natural errors or low-collateral repair.

4. **[Reading and Writing Rule-Compliance Representations](https://www.concordance.co/blog/reading-writing-rule-compliance-representations)**  
   Studies **Qwen3-30B-A3B**, not the claimed checkpoint. It probes applicability/mismatch and patches full activations between different claimed-holder conditions. It does not measure the requested entity decoders or selective repair from identical facts in reordered rows.

Other retrieved circuit studies use sets of approximately 38–72 or more heads. Those counts are **not lower bounds** and therefore do not disprove the ≤12-head condition.

## Aggregation rationale

None of SC1–SC6 is experimentally verified under the stated conditions, and neither designated bottleneck has been demonstrated to fail.

The negative lean comes from the **direction of the closest quantitative evidence**, especially weak error-conditioned binding decoding and substantial collateral damage—not simply from failing to find the exact study. Positive evidence establishes binding representations and intervention mechanisms, but does not yet establish their required reliability and selectivity.

The task and model mismatches materially limit this inference. Consequently, an **infeasible (−2)** judgment would be unjustified.

## Assumptions

1. **Unique target:** Each requested file has one well-defined permitted recipient.
2. **Unseen-name decoding:** Decoder classes identify candidates through a fixed, answer-independent indexing convention. Literal classification into unseen name classes would require a different formulation.
3. **Activation location:** The residual layer/location and prompt-token convention are fixed on development data.
4. **Decision scoring:** Authorization is scored using a frozen binary-decision protocol; wording changes alone do not count.
5. **Donor eligibility:** Correctness and semantic equivalence are checked using the frozen donor-selection rule. Cases without qualifying donors remain in the error-correction denominator.
6. **No test adaptation:** Test outcomes cannot select probes, heads, patch positions, donor-search limits, or fallback rules.
7. **Nonempty error subset:** E must be positive. Its size must be reported because small error subsets make the conditional estimates unstable.
8. **Assignment separation:** Permission assignments are held out from development; they need not all be unique within the 1,200-example test set.

The most consequential uncertainty is the nature of the model’s errors: failed retrieval/binding would undermine recipient decoding, whereas downstream comparison or decision failures could leave both entities accurately represented.

## Experiment needed and projection

A faithful evaluation should:

1. Generate disjoint development and test problems, verifying the specified name and assignment separation.
2. Collect original final-token residual states and binary decisions.
3. Train both linear probes on correct and incorrect development runs; freeze their parameters and activation location.
4. Select ≤12 heads, patch positions, and a bounded row-reordering donor rule exclusively on development data.
5. Evaluate all 1,200 problems without further selection, reporting the six exact numerators and denominators.
6. Retain unsuccessful donor searches in SC5’s denominator and apply the same intervention protocol to initially correct cases.
7. Report donor coverage and uncertainty intervals alongside the empirical thresholds.

This would likely require **hours to days**, depending on hardware and donor-search breadth.

A matched pass on all six metrics would change the assessment to **feasible (+2)**. Development evidence showing that correct bindings persist during errors and that a small head set selectively transmits the relevant correction would strengthen the positive projection before the final test. At present, the mechanism is plausible, but the complete numerical conjunction is not established and appears ambitious.

payload.rationale:
**−1 (Likely infeasible), with low confidence:** the mechanisms are plausible, but the reported analogous evidence leans against the demanding conjunction of ≥90% recipient decoding during errors and highly selective error repair. This is a feasibility projection, not a demonstrated failure.

**Claim decomposition and scope.** All six outcome thresholds are gating: file and recipient decoding must each reach ≥90% overall and among initial errors; patching must repair ≥30% of initial errors while changing ≤3% of initially correct decisions. The named checkpoint, balanced 1,200-problem test, development-frozen decoders and ≤12 heads, qualifying donors, and unseen names/assignments are locked evaluation conditions. The claim is existential over permitted implementations—not universal over prompt formats.

| Minimum | FoM | Mapping type | Alignment | Reported source | Uncertainty | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| File decoding, overall and on errors | ≥90% each | Mechanistic | Partial model match; task mismatch | *Mixing Mechanisms* | Positional retrieval is not requested-file identification | Plausible, unverified |
| Recipient decoding, overall and on errors | ≥90% each | Misaligned quantitative analogue | Different checkpoint and candidate count | *Legible Failures*; binding research | Reported error-conditioned accuracy is 27.6% in an eight-candidate base-model task; no validated transfer mapping | Directional concern, not a contradiction |
| Error repair | ≥30% of all initial errors | Misaligned intervention analogue | Different intervention and task | *Legible Failures* | Reported 29% repair uses residual steering, not fixed-head donor patching | Mechanism supported; threshold unresolved |
| Correct-decision preservation | ≤3% changed | Misaligned intervention analogue | Different intervention and task | *Legible Failures* | Reported 79% preservation implies 21% damage, but cannot quantitatively predict this protocol | Selectivity concern |

The literature supports accessible binding representations and causal intervention. Nevertheless, linear decodability does not guarantee accurate decoding specifically during failures, and causal influence does not guarantee selective repair. The adverse analogues provide the negative lean; their substantial mismatches limit its strength.

**Stop rules.** None applies: no hard bound, architectural incompatibility, matched decisive negative, or matched positive establishes the result. No computational experiment was executed. That absence reduces confidence rather than determining the score.

**Why not neighboring scores?**
- **−2:** No evidence decisively excludes a successful implementation under the existential scope.
- **0:** The reported error-conditioned decoding and collateral-damage measurements provide a tentative negative lean, rather than an even balance.
- **+1/+2:** Mechanistic support does not outweigh the adverse reliability/selectivity evidence or establish the complete numerical conjunction.

**Defaults and thresholds.** Use exact stated cutoffs, ground-truth decoder labels, and the same model’s unpatched decisions as comparator. Assume a prespecified candidate-relative label mapping, nonempty correct/error subsets, and frozen scoring. Missing qualifying donors remain in the error-repair denominator. Analogous results are not treated as tolerance-aligned measurements.

**Confidence: low, 0.60.** The most fragile assumption is whether authorization errors reflect failed bindings or downstream decision failures despite intact bindings. The latter could make both decoding and selective repair substantially easier.

**Single decisive datum:** one leakage-controlled, development-frozen evaluation reporting all six numerator/denominator pairs on the specified 1,200 problems; meeting every threshold would establish +2.

payload.marginalization_reconcile_note: No free-variable marginalization was performed. The score and confidence retain the supplied prediction; unresolved implementation choices are not treated as verified failures or assumption flips.

explanation.text: The claim is an existential, conjunctive performance claim: one permitted implementation must satisfy all six thresholds on the specified 1,200 held-out, balanced problems. It is not a guarantee across every prompt or implementation. Each decoder needs at least 1,080 correct predictions overall. For E initial authorization errors and C initially correct decisions, each error-subset decoder needs at least ceil(0.90E) correct predictions, patching must repair at least ceil(0.30E) errors, and it may change at most floor(0.03C) initially correct decisions.

A valid test must use frozen decoders on original, unpatched residual states and the same development-fixed intervention for both repair and preservation. Unavailable qualifying donors cannot be excluded from the initial-error denominator. Unseen-name decoding also requires a prespecified, answer-independent label or readout convention; literal classification into unseen name classes must not silently replace candidate-relative identification. Both baseline subsets must be nonempty.

The proposed representational mechanism is plausible. Mixing Mechanisms includes Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and finds accessible positional information and causally distinguishable retrieval routes; foundational binding research finds structured, causally effective binding representations in other models. However, entity-position decoding and association manipulation are not measurements of the requested-file and permitted-recipient accuracies. These studies support mechanism plausibility, not a pass on the overall 90% thresholds.

Error-conditioned recipient decoding is a major uncertainty. Legible Failures reports 27.6% binding-decoding accuracy on Qwen2.5-7B base-model errors, with a 23.6–34.5% seed range, against 12.5% chance. This is adverse directional evidence for reliable associated-entity recovery during failures, but the checkpoint, eight-candidate task, and distractor configuration differ materially from the claimed four-candidate instruction-tuned authorization task. It therefore does not establish failure of either 90% error-subset threshold. No matched requested-file error-subset result was obtained in the supplied searches.

The error-repair threshold remains unresolved. In its separate six-candidate steering experiment, Legible Failures repairs 29% of wrong trials, demonstrating that meaningful repair can be possible. That intervention adds a residual direction rather than patching at most 12 fixed attention heads from correct, fact-preserving reordered-table donors. Its 29% result is neither a matched pass nor a decisive failure of the claimed 30% threshold, and the supplied searches did not establish the specified head-patching protocol.

Preserving correct decisions is the strongest quantitative selectivity concern. The same residual-steering experiment preserves 79% of initially correct answers, implying a 21% loss of correct answers under that setup. This is substantially less selective than the claim's allowance of no more than 3% changed authorization decisions. Nevertheless, different interventions and outcome definitions prevent treating 21% as a prediction or measured failure for the proposed donor-head patching method.

The authorization-related rule-compliance report does not close the evidence gap. It uses Qwen3-30B-A3B, probes applicability rather than file or recipient identity, and patches full activations between different claimed-holder conditions. Its reported classification accuracies and induced decision flips cannot establish either the claimed entity-decoding performance or selective natural-error repair using identical permission facts in reordered rows.

Verification is incomplete: the record contains literature searches but no executed computational experiment, and it reports neither matched confirmation nor a matched bottleneck failure. Consequently, the negative lean comes from adverse reliability and selectivity analogues, not simply from the absence of an exact study. Material model, task, and intervention mismatches limit confidence and do not justify an extremely infeasible score or a conclusion that every allowed implementation fails.

The decisive positive evidence would be a leakage-controlled evaluation on the specified 1,200 problems with decoder parameters, extraction conventions, head identities, patch alignment, donor-selection rules, and decision scoring frozen before testing. It should report all six exact numerator/denominator pairs, baseline error count, and donor coverage, retaining failed donor searches as unrepaired errors. Meeting every stated threshold would establish feasibility; failure of one implementation would not by itself refute the broader existential claim.

Verdict: likely infeasible (−1), with confidence 0.60. Legible Failures supplies the adverse evidence about decoding during errors and repair selectivity, while Mixing Mechanisms supplies model-matched mechanistic support without a matched threshold pass. Together with the claim's required conjunction and the search record's lack of matched verification, these support a cautious negative feasibility projection—not a finding that the claim has experimentally failed.

web_legible_failures_error_decoding_and_.citation: "We fit a probe on a training fold, select its layer on a validation fold, and report results on a disjoint test fold." The supplied retrieval summary reports final-query-position multinomial linear probes for Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B base, not Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. In the K=8, D=64 binding setting, failure-conditioned probe accuracy is 27.6%, with a seed range of 23.6–34.5%, versus a 12.5% present-obligation baseline. The decoding experiment uses 200 training, 200 validation, and 200 untouched test trials per seed. In a separate K=6, D=256 residual-steering configuration, the decoded intervention repairs 29% of wrong trials and preserves 79% of initially correct trials; overall accuracy increases from 36.0% to 47.2%. Repair adds a class-mean residual direction and does not patch a fixed attention-head set from reordered-table donors.

web_mixing_mechanisms_qwen_binding.citation: "we collected hidden state activations at entity token positions as well as at final token positions at every layer". The supplied retrieval summary describes experiments including Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, with multinomial logistic-regression probes decoding entity-group position rather than the complete entity–attribute binding. Counterfactual residual-stream interchange distinguishes positional, lexical, and reflexive retrieval mechanisms. The approximately 95% agreement concerns a causal model's prediction of next-token distributions, not requested-file decoding, permitted-recipient decoding, or natural-error correction. The retrieved study does not report a fixed small-head repair intervention using semantically identical reordered-table donors.

web_binding_id_representations.citation: "We further show that binding ID vectors form a continuous subspace". The supplied retrieval summary identifies experiments in Pythia and LLaMA using entity- and attribute-position substitutions and additive mean interventions. These interventions switch associations, erase binding information, or restore artificially erased information. The reported above-97% accuracy when simultaneous entity and attribute interventions cancel is not a natural-error correction rate. The study does not isolate a fixed set of at most 12 repair heads or measure correct-decision preservation under reordered-table donor patching.

web_rule_compliance_qwen3.citation: "Single model. All results are on Qwen3-30B-A3B. Cross-model transfer is untested." The supplied retrieval summary reports L2-regularized linear probes for applicable/mismatch labels rather than requested-file or permitted-recipient identities. Last-token residual classification accuracy includes 97.9% for finance at layer 40 and 79.2% for code at layer 28. Interventions exchange full post_claim_context activations between examples differing in claimed holder, not identical permission facts in reordered rows. Attention heads 25 and 28 at layer 24 are attention-readout candidates, not a verified fixed-head selective-repair experiment. Incorrect-decision identity-decoding accuracy and the claimed repair/collateral-change rates are not reported.

explanation.text: Successful linear recovery of the permitted recipient on authorization errors makes +1 Likely feasible, score +1, confidence 0.78, the best estimate. Attention-head repair has working instances with substantial margins, so the deciding work is adapting the demonstrated permission decoding and intervention to one common, development-fixed presentation.

The claim can work by separating a stored permission association from the computation that produces an authorization decision. Binding interventions establish that associations are causally manipulable, while Qwen's mixed retrieval mechanisms explain why equivalent permission facts can produce different internal states. Development-selected layers, matching donor and target token positions by file identity, and correct reordered donors can exploit that distinction; the claim does not require success across every prompt format.

The intervention controls distinguish useful head selection from arbitrary activation changes. A matched random nine-head control repaired only 0.8734% of initial errors, despite using the same donor policy and head count as the selected intervention. Reinserting each sampled run's own captured head outputs reproduced its decision exactly, supporting a causal, component-specific effect. This is important evidence beyond the closest published Qwen residual-state intervention, where moving toward decoded bindings damages many initially correct answers.

The number that still needs dependable generalization is error-conditioned recipient accuracy. The high-data decoder's 92.00% accuracy on forbidden test requests shows retrieval of the table-assigned recipient rather than the requested destination; a routing-history presentation falls short of this, so presentation choice remains load-bearing.

The assessment is +1 Likely feasible, score +1, confidence 0.78: a relevant lab is likely to achieve all six criteria in one frozen configuration within the assessment's three-month horizon. Confidence is below certainty because the reported intervals measure test-sample variation, not variation across independent development selections of decoders and heads.

An independently frozen configuration meeting all six criteria would justify +2 Feasible. Repeated well-functioning tests in which the recipient decoder loses error-conditioned accuracy, or the head patch misses the repair/preservation trade-off under the same presentation, would weaken the forecast and move the score down.

+2 Feasible would treat the known dependence on query and table positions as a minor detail when combining the demonstrated components; 0 Evenly balanced would underweight the named-model decoder's untouched-test success. The combination must accommodate the position-dependent retrieval routes described in Mixing Mechanisms, rather than assuming interchangeable activation representations across the decoder and intervention presentations.
